title: How Hostage Negotiation Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how hostage negotiation works, covering the phases of a hostage situation (initial assault, standoff/negotiation, resolution), negotiator tactics such as stalling, lessening demands, keeping hostage takers calm, and getting hostages to interact with takers. They discuss the Munich 1972 Olympics attack, the Stockholm syndrome origin in a 1973 bank robbery (the episode says 1981 Stockholm), the Dutch train hostage incident, Russian non-negotiation cases (2002 Moscow theater, 2004 Beslan school), the 1980 Prince's Gate siege in London, and the 1975 Kuala Lumpur US consulate siege. The episode closes with a Kiva lending team plug, blog mention, and sign-off. The episode also includes a short pre-show promo for a Punkin Chunkin TV show and a Camry ad.
topics: Kuala Lumpur US consulate hostage siege 1975

segments.title: Opening banter and Punkin Chunkin promo
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about a Punkin Chunkin TV special and movies about hostages, including Dog Day Afternoon and Inside Man, and set up the topic.

segments.title: Why hostages are used and the Munich example
segments.summary: Hostage takers usually want something, and the real target is often a third party. Hostages are symbolic bargaining chips, illustrated by the 1972 Munich Olympics attack on Israeli athletes.

segments.title: Phases of a hostage situation
segments.summary: The initial violent phase, the longer standoff/negotiation phase with police involvement, and the resolution phase (surrender, assault, or granted demands). The Munich crisis ended in a bloodbath.

segments.title: Why the negotiator is not the commander
segments.summary: The negotiator must focus on talking the hostage taker down, and separating the negotiator from command lets them stall by claiming they need approval from someone else.

segments.title: Stalling with minute details and gathering information
segments.summary: Negotiators prolong situations by focusing takers on trivial details, and gather information about the taker's identity, number of takers, and mental state. Domestic disputes are the most common hostage scenario.

segments.title: Keeping hostages safe, calm, and interacting
segments.summary: Negotiators aim to lessen demands, keep hostages safe and reduce numbers, keep the situation calm, and have hostages perform tasks like fetching pizza so takers see them as human. A Dutch train hostage case shows the risk of this; the Baader-Meinhof group is mentioned as a source of early terrorism tactics.

segments.title: Stockholm syndrome
segments.summary: Stockholm syndrome is described as hostages identifying with their captors, arising from a bank robbery standoff where hostages helped the robber; psychological causes include feeling powerless and relief after survival.

segments.title: Non-negotiating countries and Russian sieges
segments.summary: The US, Russia, and Israel are described as non-negotiating; France negotiated and was targeted. Russia's 2002 Moscow theater and 2004 school sieges by Chechen separatists are discussed, with heavy hostage deaths.

segments.title: Prince's Gate siege and Kuala Lumpur consulate
segments.summary: The 1980 Prince's Gate siege in London ended with an SAS assault after negotiators stalled; a 1975 Kuala Lumpur US consulate siege saw a junior officer end up negotiating directly.

segments.title: Kiva plug and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts plug the Stuff You Should Know Kiva lending team, mention the blog, listener email address, and close the episode with an ad.
